say: In a green valley in central Vietnam, red brick towers rise out of the jungle. Some of them are more than a thousand years old.
The people who built them ruled parts of this coast for more than a thousand years. Their kingdom was called Chahm-pah.
It was a sea power that traded with China and sacked a Vietnamese capital. Its name even lived on in China, as the name of a rice.
Today, Chahm-pah has no capital and no state. But its people are still here.
This is the story of how Chahm-pah rose, how it ended, and what remains.
The Chahm spoke an Austronesian language. Its closest relatives are not Vietnamese or Khmer, but languages like Ah-chay-neez and Malay, spoken across the sea.
Chinese histories describe a kingdom on this coast called Lin-yee, from roughly the second or third century C E. Whether Lin-yee was Chahm-pah itself is still debated.
Chahm-pah was not always a single unified state. Some historians describe several regional centers along the coast, sometimes united and sometimes rivals.
Indra-poora in the north. Vee-jaya. Kow-tah-rah. And Pahn-doo-rahng-gah, in the dry far south.
These centers grew at river mouths, facing the sea. Chinese records describe Chahm traders bringing ivory, rhinoceros horn and fragrant aloeswood.
Their harbors lay along sea routes linking China and the Indian Ocean. Ships from both worlds stopped on this coast.
Chahm rulers built in fired red brick, decorated with carved sandstone. Their temple towers still stand along the coast.
Many were dedicated to Shiva, a Hindu god. At Mee Sun, inscriptions honor Bhad-raysh-vara, a form of Shiva named after an early king, Bhadra-varman.
But Chahm-pah was not only Hindu. In the ninth century, a large Buddhist monastery was established at Dong Zuong.
Inscriptions were written in Sanskrit, the classical language of India, and in Old Chahm, the language of the Chahm.
One Old Chahm stone, from Dong Yen Chow, is often described as one of the oldest known texts in any Austronesian language. Its exact date is still studied.
Further south, at Kow-tah-rah, the Chahm worshipped a goddess at the towers of Poh Nah-gar. We will come back to her.
Mee Sun is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Some of its towers were damaged during the Vietnam War.
Chahm-pah's name traveled further than its ships. In Song China, farmers grew a rice known as Chahm-pah rice.
Song records describe Chahm-pah rice as a variety that ripened early and could survive with less water.
Song records, as discussed by historian Ho Ping-tee, say that in ten twelve Emperor Jen-zong ordered thirty thousand bushels of seed from Foo-jen to be shared out in the Yahng-zuh and Huai regions.
The rice had probably reached southern China earlier, by sea. Ho argued it helped China grow far more food. Others think its effect was slower and more local.
Where did it come from first? A 2011 genetic study links these varieties to a rice group from South Asia. Chahm-pah may have been one stop on its journey, but the name stuck: Chahm-pah rice.
Chahm-pah was also a military power, and it fought neighbors on both sides.
To the west lay the Khmer empire of Angkor. In the conventional account, a Chahm force attacked Angkor in eleven seventy-seven. Historian Michael Vickery doubts parts of that story.
Khmer forces under Jaya-varman the Seventh later campaigned in parts of Chahm-pah.
To the north lay Dye Vee-et, the Vietnamese kingdom of the Red River. Here too, wars ran both ways.
Chahm inscriptions, Vietnamese chronicles and Chinese records each tell these wars from their own side.
In ten sixty-nine, Dye Vee-et's king Lee Tahn Tong captured the Chahm king. Vietnamese chronicles say three northern districts were given up for his release.
In thirteen oh-six, a Chahm king married a Vietnamese princess, Hwen Chun. In the Vietnamese chronicles, two more districts passed to Dye Vee-et with the marriage.
Then the tide turned. In the late fourteenth century, a Chahm king the Vietnamese called Cheh Bong Ngah led attack after attack to the north.
In thirteen seventy-one, Chahm forces sacked Tahng Long, the capital of Dye Vee-et.
His campaigns went on for almost twenty years, until he was killed in battle in thirteen ninety. His real Chahm name is not known.
After his death, the balance of power slowly turned against Chahm-pah.
In fourteen seventy-one, Dye Vee-et's emperor Lay Tahn Tong led a large army south against Vee-jaya, the Chahm capital.
The city fell. The Chahm king, called Chah Twahn in Vietnamese records, was captured with his family.
Vee-jaya became a major Chahm capital around the eleventh century. Chahm towers still stand near the city of Kwee Nyun.
How many died? The sources do not agree. The Vietnamese court chronicle claims over forty thousand killed and over thirty thousand captured. Those are its own figures, not a settled count.
The Ming history, written in China, records the king and more than fifty of his relatives taken away.
The northern lands of Vee-jaya became part of Dye Vee-et. Further south, smaller Chahm kingdoms survived.
A Chahm envoy told the Ming court that Annam had sacked and occupied their country.
According to Ming records, the court sent orders to Annam. Vee-jaya was never returned to Chahm rule.
For the Chahm, the heartland of their northern kingdoms was gone.
After fourteen seventy-one, Chahm-pah lived on in the south, smaller with each century.
The Nwin lords, who ruled southern Dye Vee-et, moved their frontier step by step: Foo Yen around sixteen eleven, Kow-tah-rah in sixteen fifty-three.
In the sixteen-nineties they took Pahn-doo-rahng-gah, the last Chahm principality. After resistance, they let a Chahm ruler govern it again, under Nwin authority.
Vietnamese settlement spread into lands that had been Chahm territory.
For more than a century, Pahn-doo-rahng-gah kept Chahm rulers, and its court kept records in the Chahm script.
In eighteen thirty-two, Emperor Min Mahng ended that arrangement and brought Pahn-doo-rahng-gah under direct rule, as a province of Vietnam.
Revolts followed, and were put down by eighteen thirty-five. Chahm poems from those years recorded the new rules, and how they changed Chahm life.
A kingdom that had faced the sea for more than a thousand years ended as a state.
It is tempting to ask what might have been. But history has no "if". It has only what happened, and what remains.
And what remains is a people. Vietnam's twenty nineteen census counted about a hundred and seventy-nine thousand Chahm, and Chahm communities also live in Cambodia.
Some follow a Hindu-based tradition, some Bah-nee, some Sunni Islam. Their own script, Ah-kar Trah, is still taught in some village schools.
Each year, Chahm communities celebrate Kah-tay at towers such as Poh Klong Gah-rye. Vietnam recognized the festival as national intangible heritage in 2017.
Chahm women still shape pottery by hand, walking around the clay instead of turning a wheel. UNESCO listed their craft in 2022.
At Poh Nah-gar, Chahm worshippers honor the goddess Poh Ee-nah Nah-gar. Vietnamese pilgrims honor her too, as Tee-en Ee Ah Nah, in the same towers.
And in Chahm homes, festival tables still carry their own dishes, like the ginger cakes offered to the ancestors.
The kingdom ended. Its people, its gods and its towers did not.
